query: For a damaged high-value component made from a material whose physical and microstructural characteristics make traditional fusion-welding repair ineffective because of hot-cracking risk, what intervention could enable continued service without replacing the entire part under aggressive operating conditions? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to traditional fusion-welding repair, the relevant operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Friction stir processing (FSP) as a pre-weld treatment can reduce the susceptibility to solidification cracking during fusion welding of high-strength aluminum alloys, such as AA6061, by refining the grain structure in the fusion zone and heat-affected zone.
generation.material_initial_state: High-strength aluminum alloy (AA6061) with a thickness of 3 mm
generation.intervention: Friction stir processing (FSP) as a pre-weld treatment
generation.conditions: Autogenous tungsten inert gas (TIG) welding with a welding speed of 2 mm/s, a voltage of 10 V, a current of 120 A, and a gas flow rate of 14 L/min
generation.structural_mediator: Grain size and structure in the fusion zone and heat-affected zone
generation.mechanism: Refining the grain structure in the fusion zone and heat-affected zone, which reduces the susceptibility to solidification cracking
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced susceptibility to solidification cracking during fusion welding of AA6061
generation.baseline: Traditional fusion welding without FSP pre-weld treatment
generation.boundary: Operating conditions: aggressive operating conditions, Test boundaries: tensile testing, optical microscopy, and scanning electron microscopy
generation.uncertainty: The effectiveness of FSP pre-weld treatment in reducing solidification cracking may vary depending on the specific alloy composition, welding parameters, and operating conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Comparative study of fusion welding with and without FSP pre-weld treatment on AA6061 alloy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the results show no significant difference in solidification cracking between the two conditions, the hypothesis is falsified

The susceptibility to liquation cracking is highly governed by the initial microstructure of the base metal. The extent of liquation is influenced by the grain size, second phase characteristics (i.e., nature, size and volume fraction) in the initial microstructure of the base material,.
Friction stir processing (FSP) is an effective method for locally altering the microstructure of alloys, thereby improving their localized properties. Mousavizade et al. proposed the use of FSP as a pre-weld treatment prior to fusion welding, providing a viable solution to reduce liquation cracking in the IN738 nickel-based superalloy by developing a liquation-resistant microstructure within the partially melted zone (PMZ). This technique has since been applied to enhance the weldability of various nickel-based superalloys, as well as aluminum, and magnesium alloys. For instance, Pirjamadi et al. explored the influence of FSP pre-weld treatment on cracking during the fusion welding of AA7075 alloy. They discovered that t

welding to refine grain size in the PMZ, thus eliminating the risk of liquation cracking. However, less attention has been given to the impact of FSP pre-weld treatment on solidification cracking. Given that FSP-treated samples exhibit a refined grain structure in both the heat-affected zone (HAZ) and PMZ, and considering the role of epitaxial growth in autogenous welds, this process also influences grain size in the fusion zone (FZ), thereby affecting solidification cracking. Rule et al. indicated that FSP pre-weld treatment can reduce grain size in the fusion zone of IN600 nickel-based superalloy; however, the effect on solidification cracking was not addressed.
The objective of this study is to examine the influence of FSP pre-weld treatment on the cracking phenomena during arc fusion welding of AA6061. This alloy is notably susceptible to solidification cracking but less so to liquation cracking compared to other high-strength aluminum alloys. The findings of the present study suggest that FSP pre-weld treatment enhances resistance to solidification cracking during fusion welding of AA6061.

Subsequently, bead-on-plate fusion welding was conducted on the FSP-treated samples, which were prepared using abrasive papers to achieve smoothness. The TIG welding was performed under conditions similar to those used for the untreated material. This welding strategy, which combines friction stir processing (FSP) as a pre-weld treatment followed by TIG welding, is referred to as FTIG (see Fig. 1a).
For optical microscopy, samples were sectioned perpendicular to the welding direction and subjected to standard metallographic preparation procedures to achieve a mirror finish surface. The specimens were then etched with Barker’s reagent for optical microscopy examination. The grain size within the fusion zone (FZ) was measured using the intercept method, under the ASTM E112-10 standard. For field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) analysis, the samples were etched with a 10% NaOH solution to enhance microstructural visibility.
